Field surveys targeting pre-spawning aggregations on the continental shelf off Namibia yielded gonadosomatic indices (GSI) averaging approximately 31% [GSI = approximately 31%] at a temperature of 10.2 °C [T = 10.2 °C]. Histological examination of the ovaries indicated that females with a total length of 40 centimetres [Lp = 40 centimetres] possess developing oocytes, suggesting that the onset of puberty coincides with this body size. This length at sexual maturation is considerably smaller than the species ultimate length, which has been confirmed from both commercial trawl bycatch and dedicated research surveys to reach 100 centimetres [Li = 100 centimetres]. The protracted pre-reproductive growth phase, during which individuals more than double their length after the onset of gonadal activity, likely buffers against recruitment variability in an environment characterised by sporadic prey availability and strong oceanographic seasonality.

The earliest life stages of Lophius vomerinus are exceptionally vulnerable and exhibit a minute body size that underscores the profound demographic bottleneck faced by pelagic spawners. Extrapolating from the well-documented egg diameter of a congeneric species, Lophius piscatorius, the wet weight at birth for L. vomerinus is estimated at approximately 0.00018 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.00018 grams]. Newly hatched yolk-sac larvae, still entirely endotrophic, absorb their endogenous yolk reserves during a brief lecithotrophic phase before the onset of exogenous feeding. This minuscule initial mass, among the smallest recorded for any commercially harvested teleost in southern African waters, implies that survival through the larval period is heavily dependent on the spatiotemporal match between hatching events and the blooms of small copepods that serve as first prey. The elevated mortality associated with such a small body size is partially offset by high fecundity, a classic trade-off in the life history of broadcast-spawning fishes that produce pelagic eggs.

As these yolk-sac larvae progress through the pelagic larval phase, a series of critical morphological transformations begins. Following the absorption of the yolk, the free-swimming larva must successfully capture its first planktonic prey; failure to do so within a matter of days typically results in irreversible starvation, a phenomenon known as the point of no return. Surviving individuals undergo larval metamorphosis, during which the characteristic flattened head and angling apparatus of the adult begin to take form, and the post-larval fish shifts toward a benthic existence. The transition from a planktonic existence to a demersal lifestyle is marked by a pronounced allometric shift, and the recently settled juvenile then enters a prolonged sub-adult phase. This decadal lifespan is notably extended relative to other benthic piscivores of comparable asymptotic size, and it imposes a life-history strategy centred on delayed reproduction and repeated spawning events across multiple seasons.
